Review header

This record documents the Legal & Regulatory review of the Downy Ultra comparative softness claim stack completed on 31 March 2026 by Marisol Quintero, Legal & Regulatory Counsel, Fabric & Home Care. It is the marked-up version referenced in the reviewer's 31 March 09:29 ET email to Yusuf Demir and Michael Reyes and is issued separately from that message.

The review covers the primary superiority claim, the secondary attribute ladder (fiber gentleness, sustainability, water savings) and the substantiation relied upon for each. The benchmark product is Snuggle Blue Sparkle, manufactured by Henkel Corporation. Comparative testing was performed by Ashford Textile Testing Laboratories, Inc., 1450 Gateway Industrial Drive, Suite 120, Greensboro, NC 27407 (A2LA accredited, certificate no. 4187.02) under report reference ATTL-2026-03-1188 (testing 2026-02-16 to 2026-03-13).

Claim family: Downy Ultra comparative softness — 'Softer Than Snuggle' attribute ladder
Benchmark product: Snuggle Blue Sparkle (manufacturer: Henkel Corporation)
Substantiation pack: CMK-SUB-2026-0412 v1.2, issued 2026-03-30 — owner: Samantha 'Sam C.' Cole, Consumer & Market Knowledge
Third-party laboratory: Ashford Textile Testing Laboratories, Inc. — report ATTL-2026-03-1188
Issue tracker entry: CLM-2026-0788 (Wave 2 clearance — status: open, owner M. Quintero, target 2026-04-03)
Agency of record: Saatchi & Saatchi, 375 Hudson Street, Suite 900, New York, NY 10014
Review outcome: Conditional approval — see Sections 2, 3 and 4

Privileged and confidential — attorney work product. This markup supersedes the preliminary read given on 8 March 2026, which was an informal review of the attribute ladder and did not constitute formal sign-off. No claim in this stack is cleared for production until the sign-off block in Section 6 is complete.

1. Scope and questions answered

Two questions were put to the brand and agency teams on 31 March before the detailed review was undertaken. Both were answered in the same working day and the answers are recorded here because they define the boundary of this clearance.

1. Is the claim running against Snuggle specifically, or as a broader category comparison? Answer received: the claim runs against Snuggle specifically. All testing in CMK-SUB-2026-0412 v1.2 and ATTL-2026-03-1188 is head-to-head Downy Ultra versus Snuggle Blue Sparkle. There is no category-wide or 'all leading brands' dataset behind the stack, and none is planned for this campaign window.
2. What is the tolerance threshold for claim risk we are working with? Answer received and adopted: the standard comparative-superiority envelope for a substantiated head-to-head. Approval is granted within a low-to-moderate challenge-risk envelope: substantiation is sufficient to defend a NAD challenge on the narrowed Snuggle comparison, but not a broadened 'leading competitor' or 'softest' formulation. Any widening of the comparator set voids this clearance and requires re-review.

The review was completed inside the window requested by the brand team on 30 March. Preliminary thoughts were promised to Yusuf Demir and Michael Reyes by Thursday end of day, and a 15-minute huddle was offered at that point to walk through any adjustments before formal sign-off. This markup is delivered ahead of that commitment; the huddle offer stands and should be taken up only if either party disputes a marked change rather than as a routine step.

Out of scope for this record: package artwork legibility proofing (Design), media placement contracts (Media & Brand Engagement), and any non-U.S. execution. The Canadian and Mexican adaptations are handled separately and are addressed in Section 4.

2. Marked-up claim stack

The table below reproduces each claim as submitted, the wording as marked, and the reason for the change. 'Approved as marked' means the claim is cleared in the marked wording only; the original wording is not cleared and must not survive into any layout, cutdown or retail-partner asset. Struck and held claims must be removed from the working deck rather than greyed out, to prevent re-entry during creative markup.

Claim-by-claim markup — Downy Ultra 'Softer Than Snuggle' stack (review record CLR-2026-0781)
Ref | Tier | Original wording | Marked wording | Rationale | Disposition
C-01 | Primary superiority | Softer than the leading competitor. | Softer than Snuggle. | Narrows exposure by naming the benchmark actually tested. 'Leading competitor' invites a comparator set we have not tested and would put the claim outside the agreed risk envelope. Testing supports Downy Ultra versus Snuggle Blue Sparkle only. | Approved as marked
C-02 | Primary support | Superior softness. | (Struck — no substitute wording cleared at this time.) | As a standalone, unqualified phrase this reads as a formulation-level absolute rather than a head-to-head result. Cotton terry is the strongest cell (index 112 versus Snuggle = 100 after 20 wash cycles) but the re-test addendum is not yet in hand. Reconsider on receipt of ATTL-2026-03-1188-A1. | Struck pending cotton re-test
C-03 | Secondary — fabric care | Gentle on fibers. | Gentle on fibers — 96.4% fiber-strength retention after 20 wash cycles. | Retained with the wash-count qualifier attached. The bare phrase was drifting toward an open-ended durability promise; the qualifier ties it to the measured protocol and the tested cycle count. | Approved as marked
C-04 | Secondary — sustainability | Responsibly sourced. | Responsibly sourced. (Placement restricted — see condition.) | Retained, but must not appear in the same sentence, headline or on-screen frame as a softness superiority statement. Combining them implies the sustainability attribute is part of the substantiated comparison, which it is not. This addresses the ladder tension raised by the agency on 28 March: lead with one audience per execution. | Approved with placement restriction
C-05 | Secondary — sustainability | 40% less water. | (Held — requires a stated baseline, e.g. 'up to 40% less water than [named comparator/prior formulation], per [measurement basis]'.) | A percentage without a comparator is not approvable. The figure must state what it is measured against and on what basis before it can be cleared for consumer-facing use. | Held — not approvable as written
C-06 | Secondary — comparative | Outperforms the competition on every softness metric. | Preferred over Snuggle for softness by 61% of participants in a paired-preference test (n=312). | Tightening of the secondary comparative language flagged in the preliminary 8 March comment. 'Every metric' is unsupportable across the three fabric families tested; the paired-preference result is precise, sourced and defensible. | Approved as marked
C-07 | On-pack burst | Softer vs. the leading softener. | Softer vs. Snuggle. | Same narrowing as C-01, applied to the pack burst so that pack and advertising carry identical comparator language. Burst must be footnoted per Section 4. | Approved as marked
C-08 | Secondary — sensory | Consumers can feel the difference. | In sensory testing, consumers noticed a softness difference versus Snuggle. | Removes the universal 'can feel' construction and anchors the statement to the sensory work in CMK-SUB-2026-0412 v1.2. Not to be used without the C-01 footnote in the same execution. | Approved as marked

Editorial note for the agency: where a layout previously carried 'leading competitor' inside body copy, the replacement is 'Snuggle' without qualifiers such as 'the leading brand Snuggle' or 'category leader Snuggle'. Adding a superiority descriptor to the comparator reintroduces the exposure the markup was intended to remove.

3. Substantiation conditions

Approval of the marked stack is conditional on the following three items. Each must be evidenced in the substantiation file before formal sign-off issues; two of the three are documentation fixes rather than new work.

Condition (a) — Humidity controls callout in the textile testing protocol appendix

The current protocol write-up in CMK-SUB-2026-0412 v1.2 describes wash cycles, fabric families and panel construction but omits the conditioning parameters. Conditioning materially affects hand-feel and sensory scoring, and its absence is the single most exploitable gap in the file. The appendix must carry an explicit callout in the following terms: specimens conditioned at 21°C ± 1°C and 65% ± 2% RH for a minimum of 24 hours per ASTM D1776, with the same conditioning applied to Downy Ultra and Snuggle Blue Sparkle specimens in each cell. The callout is to be added by the substantiation owner and countersigned by the third-party laboratory.

Condition (b) — Baseline for any water-savings figure

Claim C-05 is held. No consumer-facing execution may carry '40% less water' or any variant of it until the baseline is stated in the claim itself and documented in the substantiation file: what the saving is measured against, over what usage cycle, and on what measurement basis. A figure with an internal baseline that is not disclosed on the face of the claim is not approvable. If the sustainability pillar is needed in the June creative, use the recycled-content proof point (50% post-consumer recycled HDPE in the refill bottle; 30% PCR in the refill pouch film), which is separately documented, rather than the water figure.

Condition (c) — Wave 2 validation and laboratory independence cited in the footnote

The Wave 2 sensory validation and the independence of the testing laboratory must be cited in the claim footnote and in the substantiation index, not merely held on the shared drive. Holding the evidence is not the same as citing it; a challenge is answered from the face of the advertising first. The approved footnote in Section 4 discharges this condition when used verbatim.

Record note on the 22 March concern: the issue tracker shows the validation cleared in Wave 2 (entry CLM-2026-0788). The concern raised in the pod channel that week arose from an out-of-date tab in a locally saved copy of the tracker, not from a genuine gap in the file. Working copies of the tracker should be refreshed from the live entry before any further escalation on this point.

4. Approved footnote and usage rules

The following footnote text is approved verbatim for on-pack and in-advertising use wherever the comparison in C-01, C-07 or C-08 appears. It may not be paraphrased, shortened, split across frames or moved to a landing page in place of on-asset display.

Approved footnote (verbatim): "Softer than Snuggle. Based on independent third-party laboratory softness testing of Downy Ultra vs. Snuggle Blue Sparkle on cotton, cotton-blend and synthetic fabrics after 20 wash cycles under controlled conditioning (21°C / 65% RH). Individual results vary by fabric and wash conditions."

Legibility specification: the footnote must appear at minimum 8 pt in print and 14 px in digital, at no less than 70% contrast against background, and must appear in the first frame in which the claim is spoken or shown in video.

Territory: cleared for use in the United States and Puerto Rico only. Not cleared for Canada or Mexico; French-language substantiation and Canadian comparative-advertising review are pending.

Channel usage rules for the narrowed comparison (C-01 / C-07 / C-08)
Channel / format | Comparison permitted | Conditions
Retail media — Walmart Connect, Amazon Ads, Kroger Precision Marketing, Roundel | Yes | Footnote on the creative unit itself at 14 px minimum, 70% contrast. Retailer-hosted disclosure pages do not satisfy the requirement.
Streaming / CTV, 30-second and 15-second cutdowns | Yes | Footnote burned into the first frame in which the claim is spoken or shown and held for the duration of the claim.
Six-second cutdowns and bumper units | No | The footnote cannot be displayed legibly at this length. Use a non-comparative softness message in six-second adaptations. This resolves the short-form adaptation concern raised on 6 March against creative directions 1 and 2.
Audio and radio | No | No means of carrying the visual footnote; a spoken abbreviation of the footnote is not approved.
Social static, carousel and paid social video (10s+) | Yes | Footnote in-asset, not in caption or comments. Caption-only disclosure is not accepted.
In-store POS, shelf talkers, aisle violators | Yes | Footnote at 8 pt minimum in print. Shelf talkers below the size that can carry 8 pt must use a non-comparative message.
On-pack (front-of-pack burst, back-of-pack copy) | Yes | C-07 burst must be footnoted on the same panel. Sustainability copy (C-04) must sit on a different panel or a clearly separated block.
Influencer, earned media and PR talking points | No, without pre-clearance | Route proposed wording to Legal & Regulatory before briefing any third party; unscripted repetition of the comparison is not covered by this clearance.
Canada and Mexico adaptations | No | Out of territory. See territory line above.

Until sign-off issues, creative markup and the move to production remain hard-blocked; that block is stated here so it is not carried as an assumption in the agency schedule. 1. Purpose and Scope

Marc asked for a perspective on the Southeast and Mountain West implications of the field-marketing centralization summary before it goes to the board, and Dave asked for retention data and engagement sentiment for the Rocky Mountain markets. This document answers both asks in one place: what the retention picture actually looks like, who we lose if we cut over in a single step, and what a phased alternative costs.

The structural assumptions used here are taken from the centralization summary as forwarded, not from anything circulating informally:

• Consolidation of 8 regional teams into 5 core zones: ZN-01 West Coast Zone, ZN-02 Mountain Zone, ZN-03 Southwest Zone, ZN-04 Central Zone, ZN-05 Northeast Zone.
• New skip-level reporting for area leads.
• Expected headcount reduction of roughly 12% across field ops: 74.0 field-marketing FTE current state to 65.0 FTE post-realignment, a net reduction of 9.0 FTE or 12.2%. Brand marketing is +2 FTE and field ops is flat over the same period.
• Q3 rollout timeline as originally scoped, with an effective date of 1 May 2026 for role changes.
• Rocky Mountain is split under the draft map: Colorado and Wyoming to ZN-02 Mountain Zone, Utah and New Mexico to ZN-03 Southwest Zone and managed remotely.
• Legacy footprint context: Southeast 512 restaurants, Rocky Mountain 203 restaurants, total 3,115 across the eight legacy regions.

2. Retention Baseline

The baseline below was pulled on the morning of 19 January 2026 from the field-marketing people dashboard and cross-checked against the HR exit-interview extract. Southeast is the headline problem. Field marketing leads in the Southeast are at 78% year-over-year retention, down from 84% the prior year — a six-point deterioration in a region that is already carrying a disproportionate share of growth. Sam Whitfield's team carries roughly 40% of quarterly growth in the region, which means the retention exposure and the revenue exposure are the same people.

Mountain West is a different failure mode. Retention there is not structurally low year-round; it collapses seasonally. We are down roughly four people in the last month, concentrated in northern Colorado and Utah, and the pattern is recurring: people give notice or simply stop showing up around mid-October when ski-season employment opens. The realignment's effective date sits immediately before the next run-up to that window, which is the single most avoidable timing error in the current plan.

The Rocky Mountain and Southwest markets also carry an intangible I want on the record. We have spent eighteen months building direct trust with field partners and store operators in those markets, and Sam Whitfield and I have both been fielding continuity questions from local operators. That relationship equity does not appear on any headcount line and is the asset most exposed by a single-step cutover.

5. Recommendation — Staggered Transitions and Retention Bonuses

Three mechanics, in priority order. Taken together they preserve the strategy while removing the churn spike.

1. (a) Stagger the role transitions rather than executing a single cutover. Role changes take effect 1 May 2026 as scheduled, but move in waves by zone and by churn profile, with full consolidation pushed to Q4. This is the recommendation Marc has already endorsed in reply, on the basis that phasing keeps us on strategy without the people risk, and Dave is incorporating it into the ops timeline.
2. (b) Fund targeted retention bonuses for the high-risk cohort. Sized within the 10–15% of base policy band, with a 12-month stay agreement and a 50% on signature / 50% at month 12 payment structure. I have modelled the cohort at 12% of base, mid-band. All comp mechanics — instrument type, clawback language, tax treatment and whether these sit inside or outside the annual bonus plan — must be validated by Sam Cole before anything is communicated to an individual.
3. (c) Preserve localized touch points in low-volume markets through at least Q3. Local-market retention resourcing is preserved through Q3 in any market cluster whose prior-year (FY2025 actual, restated onto the FY2026 zone map) aggregate AUV is below $50M, with a secondary unit-level screen at $2.6M prior-year AUV.

It is the scenario that describes what actually happens if Dr. Ramaswamy draws in December, so it is the baseline against which the other two are measured. The QBI line is therefore shown at zero rather than modeled as a variable.

8. Compliance, buy-sell and liquidity notes

Dr. Ramaswamy's condition on the deferred compensation angle — that it must be clean from a compliance perspective and must not create exposure for Bayfront down the road — is the right condition, and it is the reason the deferred arrangement is carried at zero in the Scenario 3 table. A partner's distributive share of partnership income is not employee compensation, and attempting to defer it through a nonqualified arrangement raises questions under the deferred-compensation rules as well as self-employment-tax questions. Before any dollar of that structure is assumed, it needs review by the practice's own tax counsel, and the design has to be documented at the partnership level rather than negotiated partner by partner.

On the wealth-management side, the advisor of record adds a related consideration: any deferral should be integrated with Dr. Ramaswamy's liquid asset positioning and with the buy-sell triggers at the practice, and personal liquidity needs for the coming year should be covered independently of the deferral. A deferral that is unwound early because of an unplanned cash need is worse than no deferral at all.

1. Rationale

Current density metrics suggest the Central Iowa territory has reached an inflection point at which bifurcation improves coverage velocity and dealer responsiveness rather than simply adding overhead. The territory now carries 23 enrolled dealer sites and 74 active row-crop accounts against a single territory-manager footprint, with a precision-ag rollout that reached its 60-day mark on 9 January 2026 (day zero 10 November 2025). Throughput is strong, but it is strong in a way that is beginning to consume the coverage it produces.

Three observations from the rollout performance review support the split:

• Dealer concentration in the Des Moines basin is creating scheduling bottlenecks. Site visits cluster in a narrow band along the Highway 30 and Interstate 35 corridors, and demonstration equipment moves through the same handful of yards.
• Account coverage in the western corridor is uneven. Boone and Hamilton County accounts are being serviced on a best-effort cadence rather than a planned one, and the gap shows up in onboarding and training scores more than in equipment volume.
• Central Iowa is running hot on throughput. At the 60-day snapshot, connected-sensor activation stood at 76% of eligible machines at pilot accounts while dealer-site enablement stood at 68% of the 23 sites — the machines are moving faster than the dealer network is being brought along.

The intent of the split is to right-size capacity and give each territory manager a cleaner operational footprint, with a windshield-time profile that supports a planned visit cadence instead of a reactive one. The timing is deliberately tied to the precision-ag specialization the field organisation is restructuring around: an assignment drawn now, on rollout-era data, can be built around where installer certification and precision attach revenue actually sit, rather than around historical equipment-only geography.

This paper does not address headcount, compensation plan mechanics or title changes. Any compensation-plan consequence of a boundary change is routed to HR under Section 6.

2. Option A — Proposed Geography (Primary)

Option A is the primary proposal and the version modelled in Section 4. The North zone is anchored around Story County, absorbing the existing patches currently worked by the associate territory manager, Samuel Whitfield (Employee No. JD671802); the South zone pivots on the Marshall/Jasper corridor. Polk County is divided, with the northern suburban and row-crop band assigned North and the metro-and-south band assigned South.

3. Option B — Alternate Geometry Under Discussion

An alternate geometry was circulated in a parallel note and is preserved here as a footnote rather than merged into Option A. In that framing the district is divided as Des Moines metro plus south to one manager, and Ames plus a northwest expansion zone to the other. Expressed in county terms, Option B reads: North zone — Boone, Hamilton, Hardin and Story north of Highway 30; South zone — Story south of Highway 30, Marshall, Jasper, all of Polk, Warren and Marion.

The material difference is that Option B runs the boundary through Story County along Highway 30 rather than around it. That places Ames — and with it the Ames dealer concentration, including the lead See & Spray pilot site — on the South side together with the whole of the Des Moines metro, while the North zone becomes a lighter northwest expansion territory built on Boone, Hamilton, Hardin and the Story City / Roland band.

7. Rationale Memo and Recommended Call Agenda

The reasoning behind this redline is short enough to state on one page, and Salesforce would rather state it in a conversation than in another exchange of documents.

1. Caps protect both parties. A ceiling is what makes an indemnity real. An uncapped covenant cannot be insured, cannot be reserved against, and in practice becomes a matter for litigation rather than a matter for a claims process. A stated number can be paid.
2. Indemnity should track control and known IP risk. Salesforce controls what it builds and delivers, so it stands behind third-party intellectual property claims against the Service as provided — clause 4.2(a). Salesforce does not control Customer Data, Customer configuration, Customer's combinations with non-Salesforce products, or the acts of Customer's own contractors, so those sit with Customer — clause 4.2(c).
3. Tiering by claim type is how most Salesforce enterprise agreements are structured. This is precisely the tiered approach Mr. Maddox asked for on 3 February: different ceilings for different claim types, rather than a single all-or-nothing number.
4. The twelve-months'-fees measure is favourable to a growing account. Because the cap is measured on the trailing twelve months under the applicable order form, it rises with the expansion ramp. At the full-ramp run rate of USD 170,000 per month it is approximately USD 2,040,000 — materially above the fixed figure a 2023-vintage cap would have produced.
5. The 2x concession already made is not being clawed back. The two-times-contract-value ceiling accepted by Salesforce on 1 February 2026 stands, and is recorded at clause 6.1(d) as the reference point for the general-liability tier.
6. A live walkthrough beats document ping-pong. Salesforce proposes one 45-minute call with Customer's legal and risk reviewers, with Hannah Okonkwo leading the business rationale and Renee Castaneda covering the legal reasoning, rather than a further round of marked drafts.

4.2 Diversion Controls. Covered Entity shall maintain documented controls preventing (a) transfer, resale or dispensing of 340B-priced product to any individual who is not a patient of Covered Entity, (b) commingling of 340B and non-340B inventory without an auditable virtual accumulator, and (c) duplicate discount on any unit for which a Medicaid rebate is claimed. Covered Entity shall certify quarterly, via the Attestation Addendum, that these controls were operative throughout the preceding quarter, and shall report any suspected diversion to Pfizer within one (1) business day of discovery.

4.2.1 Patient-definition criteria. For each dispensation of 340B-priced product, Covered Entity shall be able to demonstrate that (i) the individual is registered as a patient of Covered Entity and Covered Entity maintains records of that individual's care; (ii) the care was provided by a health-care professional employed by Covered Entity or under a contractual or other arrangement such that responsibility for care remains with Covered Entity; and (iii) the individual received a health-care service consistent with the service for which Covered Entity's 340B eligibility was established. Individuals seen solely under a referral arrangement in which responsibility for care does not remain with Covered Entity are not patients for purposes of this Section.

4.2.2 Contract-pharmacy tracking. Each contract-pharmacy arrangement shall be listed and dated in Exhibit A, item 5, and shall operate on a ship-to registered under DSH240918. Covered Entity shall reconcile contract-pharmacy dispensing data to the virtual accumulator not less than monthly, retain the reconciliation for five (5) years under provision 2.3, and remove from service any arrangement for which two consecutive monthly reconciliations cannot be produced.

4.2.3 Quarterly self-audit. Covered Entity shall perform a documented self-audit each calendar quarter covering not fewer than thirty (30) randomly selected 340B-priced dispensations, shall report exceptions and remediation in the Attestation Addendum, and shall retain the two most recent quarterly self-audit files for inspection under provision 2.3. The self-audit narrative shall be signed by the Financial Controller, 340B Program.

4. Block 1 — Root cause summary

The originating event is a tooling calibration drift at Spirit AeroSystems Wichita (SPR-ICT-3S) that began approximately two weeks before detection and produced panel thickness variance found at final inspection rather than in process. The Spirit maintenance log dated 14 January 2026 shows the drift starting immediately after the last tool reset, with no re-verification recorded against the reset. Spirit accepts ownership of the calibration miss. The original hold covered the non-conformances raised in shipment batch SN 4501–4512.

Table 3 — Hypothesis tracks and disposition
Track | Hypothesis | Disposition | Supporting evidence
Track 1 | Material traceability — heat-lot or mill-cert gap in the affected panels | Closed, not causal | Mill certificates and heat-lot genealogy reconciled for SN 4501–4512 with no gaps
Track 2 | Process drift in the fuselage join — operator or sequence variation | Closed, not causal | Join sequence records and shift logs consistent across the affected window; variance signature is uniform, not operator-linked
Track 3 | Tooling calibration — drift at the fuselage frame interface | CONFIRMED as root cause | Spirit maintenance log 14 January 2026; no post-reset verification; panel thickness variance profile matches drift onset

• Detection point: final inspection, not receiving inspection at Everett — the containment question is therefore how much conforming-looking stock is already forward of Wichita.
• Boeing quality position (G. Mathis): controlled re-inspection of delivered stock plus a process audit at Spirit before any line restart on the affected part numbers.
• Spirit commits to first-article re-verification on the first three lots produced after the tool is re-set and re-certified.
• Boeing source inspection (N. Khoury) will hold sign-off authority on the re-certified tool before conforming lots are released to the dock.

1. Question and Framing

The question put on the table last week is whether the poultry category chases volume or defends net-price realization into the Q4 bonus measurement period. It is not an academic framing. The bonus construct for the category sales role is measured on three components that do not move together: category volume, net-price realization, and the Walmart joint-business-plan scorecard. Volume is bought most easily with price, and every point of price bought back in trade or off-invoice comes out of realization. The two principal levers therefore pull against each other inside a single payout formula.

Against the Q4 base of $48.0M net sales on 20.6M lbs (1.72M cases), one point of net-price realization is worth approximately $480K of gross-margin dollars, because realized price flows through almost undiluted. One point of volume is worth approximately $106K of gross-margin dollars at the 22.1% category margin rate. The ratio is roughly 4.5 to 1 in favour of price. That ratio is the single most important number in this pack: it means a volume push has to be very large indeed to pay for even a modest realization give-back.

The decision required from the category team is narrow and specific. What is the realistic volume ceiling if the team stays disciplined on net-price realization — that is, the volume the field believes it can deliver without falling back on aggressive off-invoice? That number, not the modeled maximum, is what will be used to lock the Q4 stretch targets.

• Measurement components: category volume (lbs and cases); net-price realization (index vs. $2.33/lb base); Walmart JBP scorecard metrics.
• Modeled levers: list-price realization, trade-spend rate, off-invoice depth, promotional frequency, and assortment mix between premium cuts and commodity-heavy SKUs.
• Constraint carried from the category team: Q3 volume has already softened 2.3% against prior year, so the volume line starts from a weaker base than the JBP commitment assumes.
• Constraint carried from the account team: sustained pressure from the Walmart merchant organisation on net price, concentrated in commodity-heavy SKUs.
• Out of scope for this pack: individual payout calculations, plan-document eligibility language, and any beef/pork bonus construct.

Decision requested from R. Albright: the realistic volume ceiling under net-price discipline. Everything downstream in this pack — stretch targets, trade-spend rate, and the multiplier band — is set by that one input.

2. Three Scenarios

Three scenarios were modeled. Scenario A assumes a 2.5% net-price realization gain with flat volume. Scenario B holds price flat and targets a 6% volume lift. Scenario C splits the difference at 1.2% price plus 3.5% volume growth. Net-price index 100.0 equals $2.33/lb realized net; volume index 100.0 equals 20.6M lbs per quarter (82.4M lbs annualised).

B — Volume-led | 0.0% (flat) | +6.0% | 100.0 | 106.0 | 6.5% | +636 | 0.79x

The payout variance across these three is material. Scenario A nets $1.2M more in gross-margin dollars than the no-change case and $564K more than Scenario B, but it is only achievable if current SKU velocity holds — the model assumes zero volume erosion from a 2.5-point realization gain, which is generous against Circana's own-price elasticities for the category. Scenario B is the weakest of the three on margin dollars despite being the strongest on units, and it carries the compression risk: if the 6% lift has to be purchased with deeper off-invoice than the modeled 6.5% trade-spend rate, the margin delta erodes quickly and the multiplier falls with it.

4. Base-Case Recommendation and Stress Test

Rev. A.1, added the same afternoon on receipt of the category lead's reply. R. Albright's read is to weight toward Scenario C as the base case, on the grounds that it balances bonus impact against defensible margin. Two facts sit behind that call. First, Q3 volume has already softened 2.3%, so chasing volume in Q4 means recovering that softness before any of the growth counts, and the model does not credit recovery. Second, the account is under sustained net-price pressure from Christopher Vetter's Walmart sales organisation and from the merchant side, concentrated in commodity-heavy SKUs — precisely the items where realization is thinnest and elasticity highest. Conceding realization there to buy units would be the most expensive version of Scenario B.

A stress test was requested and has been run: volume growth at 2.0% instead of 3.5%, described by the category team as closer to what field reps indicate they can deliver without falling back on aggressive off-invoice. The 1.5-point volume shortfall costs $159K of gross margin on the linear grid. It does not stop there, however. At 2.0% volume the Q4 plan under-absorbs fixed conversion and distribution cost, and the modeled recovery behaviour of the field is to release incremental off-invoice late in the quarter, which lifts the effective trade-spend rate from 5.0% to 5.5%. Both effects are charged in the adjusted line below.

The stress test is the argument for setting the stretch target honestly rather than optimistically. A 1.5-point miss on volume looks small on the grid and is small on the grid — $159K — but the operating response to the miss is what does the damage, taking the adjusted gross-margin delta down to +$364K and the multiplier from 1.02x to 0.92x. If 2.0% is the number the field can actually stand behind, the correct move is to plan at 2.0% with the trade-spend rate held at 5.0% by policy, which returns a multiplier of 1.00x, rather than to plan at 3.5% and pay for the shortfall in off-invoice.

Recommendation carried into Rev. A.1: adopt Scenario C as the base case, but set the volume line at the field-supportable ceiling rather than the modeled 3.5%, and hold the trade-spend rate at 5.0% as a hard constraint rather than a planning assumption.

5. Revision Note — Blended Tiered-Discount Rerun (10 February 2026)

Pushing volume aggressively to hit the 8% growth target drops net-price realization 2.3%, which kills the margin-based bonus multiplier outright. Conversely, defending pricing and accepting 4% volume growth lands the category in the sweet spot for net-price targets but misses the volume commitment by roughly $12M. Against the annual base of 82.4M lbs (6.87M cases, $191.6M net sales), a $12M commitment gap is 5.2M lbs or 433K cases; a $6M gap is 2.6M lbs or 216K cases.

5.1 Maintenance mechanics

1. Daily mark. The Custodian marks the Pledge Sub-Account at the close of each trading day; the borrowing base is recomputed from that mark at the advance rates in §4.2.
2. Notice. If combined LTV exceeds 65% on any closing mark, Secured Party delivers a maintenance notice by end of the following business day to Pledgor, to the Family Office Contact of record and to the Controller.
3. Cure period. Five (5) business days from delivery of the maintenance notice, during which no liquidation may be initiated and no Notice of Exclusive Control may be delivered.
4. Cure options. Additional eligible collateral, cash delivery, or principal paydown, at Pledgor's election and in any combination.
5. Concentration. No single eligible position may exceed 20% of eligible collateral; a position that breaches the limit through market appreciation is not a default but is excluded from the borrowing base above the limit.
6. Escalation. Any maintenance event, cured or uncured, is reported to Morgan Reyes and to the undersigned on the day it arises, and is summarised for loan committee at the next quarterly review.

Slide 8 — Performance and Value Narrative (COMPLIANCE FLAG)

Beyond the rate action itself, the three-year structure is designed to return value to Whitcomb through the stop-loss and premium-recapture provision attaching to the disability lines. Where aggregate paid disability claims finish the plan year below the pooled attachment point, the recapture provision credits a share of the favourable margin back to the plan sponsor at the following anniversary.

This structure delivers guaranteed returns of approximately $214,000 over the three-year rate hold. (12)

• Guaranteed returns on stop-loss recapture and guaranteed renewal stability for the full 36-month term.
• Modelled on Whitcomb's own three-year paid-claims history for STD-200 and LTD-300, at a 78% target loss ratio and the pooled attachment point stated in the underwriting exhibit.
• Recapture credit applied against the following anniversary's premium rather than paid in cash, which keeps the credit outside the definition of a dividend for Connecticut filing purposes.
• Renewal stability: no re-rate in years 2 and 3 other than the ±10% enrollment-variance provision.
